findings.claim: The text of practice question 6 reads: 'Accept as LOW severity simplification if the spec only requires blow moulding for GCSE, but update the mark scheme to note that PET bottles specifically use injection stretch blow moulding...' followed by 'Explain both processes and discuss why each is more suitable for its product than the other would be.'
findings.truth: That is an editor's instruction from an earlier pass, not a question. Students see an unanswerable prompt. The mark scheme answers a question about injection moulding of a bottle cap and blow moulding of a PET bottle, so the question has been restored to match.
findings.evidence: internal: the mark scheme in the same item

findings.claim: The question 6 scheme says a PET bottle is made when 'a hot polymer parison (tube) is clamped in a split mould and compressed air inflates it'.
findings.truth: That is extrusion blow moulding, used for HDPE milk and shampoo bottles. PET bottles are made by injection stretch blow moulding: an injection-moulded preform is reheated, stretched with a rod and then blown. The lesson body already says this, so the scheme contradicted its own lesson.
findings.evidence: content_html of the same lesson (Deforming and Reforming Processes)

findings.claim: 'millions of identical cartons are die-cut each hour in automated lines', repeated in the question 5 scheme as 'very high production rate (millions per hour)'.
findings.truth: Commercial die-cutting presses run at roughly 7,000-20,000 sheets per hour. Even with many blanks per sheet the output is tens or hundreds of thousands per hour, not millions.
findings.evidence: order-of-magnitude check against flatbed and rotary die-cutter throughput

findings.claim: 'For textiles, drape forming heats thermoplastic-coated fabric over a mould to produce shaped components for upholstery and protective equipment.'
findings.truth: Drape forming is a polymer thermoforming process: a heated thermoplastic sheet, usually acrylic, is draped over a former and keeps that shape as it cools. It is not a textiles process. Pleating and gathering are the textile deforming examples the spec names.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.8 (deforming and reforming list) and 3.2.5 (textiles: sew, pleat, gather, quilt, pipe)

findings.claim: 'MIG welding is the standard commercial process for steel structures, car bodies and metal furniture frames.'
findings.truth: Car body shells are assembled mainly by robotic resistance spot welding, with thousands of spot welds per vehicle. MIG is standard for steel structures, gates and furniture frames but not for body-in-white assembly.
findings.evidence: automotive body-in-white practice; lesson 6 already says 'robotic welding assembles car bodies'

findings.claim: Question 4's scheme awards the mark only for 'The paper cup company uses continuous production'.
findings.truth: Disposable paper cups are discrete identical items made on automated lines, which is mass production. Continuous production means an unbroken flow of material such as paper, steel, chemicals or oil. A student answering 'mass production' was correct and was marked wrong, so the scheme now credits mass production and accepts continuous where the answer explains the non-stop line.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.7 (prototype, batch, mass, continuous) and the lesson's own definition of continuous production

findings.claim: The PCB passage says 'UV light hardens the resist coating where tracks are required. The unhardened resist is washed away in a developer solution, exposing the copper beneath those areas.'
findings.truth: That describes negative photoresist, which is real but is not what school and most GCSE-textbook PCB work uses. School photo-etch kits use positive resist: UV breaks down the resist it reaches, developer removes it, and the mask is opaque over the tracks. A student who learned the version in this lesson would describe the mask and the developer step backwards in an exam. Options: (a) rewrite to the positive-resist route students actually use in the workshop; (b) rewrite neutrally, for example 'UV light through a mask changes the resist so the developer removes it everywhere except the track areas, then ferric chloride etches the bare copper'; (c) leave it, since negative resist is a genuine commercial process.
findings.evidence: school photo-etch PCB practice; the spec (3.2.5) names only 'photosensitive PCB board' without specifying the chemistry
findings.ruling: Photoresist step reworded neutrally (mask + developer leaves resist over the tracks) so neither positive nor negative chemistry is asserted.

findings.claim: 'timber-based boards like MDF and chipboard are dimensionally stable and accept screws reliably'
findings.truth: Chipboard has poor screw-holding, especially into the edge, which is the reason cam locks and barrel nuts are used in flat-pack furniture instead of plain screws. The sentence uses the weak property to explain the fitting that exists because of it.
findings.evidence: internal logic of the same sentence

findings.claim: Green timber 'contains a high moisture content - up to 100% in some species'.
findings.truth: Moisture content is quoted on a dry-weight basis, so green softwood sapwood often exceeds 100% and can reach about 200%. 'Up to 100%' reads as a ceiling and is low.
findings.evidence: standard wood-drying moisture-content ranges

summary: The unit is factually sound on the technical content: the six Rs, the five stresses, heat treatments, alloy compositions, sources and conversion routes, stock forms, scales of production and finish-to-material pairings (anodising to aluminium, galvanising to steel, tanalising to timber) are all correct, and every knowledge-check key and calculation recomputes clean. The damage is in the exam framing: all nine lessons end on a 12-mark extended-response practice item that credits SPaG, neither of which exists on this paper, and lesson 9's extended question text is a leaked fact-checker instruction rather than a question. Lesson 9 also mis-assigns drape forming to textiles, names MIG as the car-body process, and overstates die-cutting throughput by orders of magnitude; lesson 6's scheme marks the correct 'mass production' answer wrong.
